vopros: What do foreign nationals need to buy a home in Los Angeles?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. A foreign national can generally buy residential real estate in Los Angeles without being a U.S. citizen or permanent resident. California does not generally impose a citizenship or immigration-status requirement simply to own a home. The practical requirements depend heavily on whether you're paying cash or financing.

For a typical purchase, you would usually need:

- Identification: A valid foreign passport and often a second form of identification. Escrow/title companies will perform identity and compliance checks.
- Funds: For a cash purchase, you'll need documented funds that can be wired into U.S. escrow. Banks and escrow companies may request evidence of the source of funds, particularly for large international transfers.
- Financing, if applicable: Foreign-national mortgages exist, but lenders commonly require more documentation and larger down payments than conventional U.S. mortgages. Requirements vary significantly by lender.
- U.S. bank account: Not legally required merely to own the property, but often very useful for escrow, mortgage payments, property taxes, insurance, HOA dues, and other expenses.
- ITIN: You don't necessarily need an Individual Taxpayer Identification Number merely to acquire the house. An ITIN can become necessary for U.S. tax filings and other tax matters. The IRS specifically notes that a foreign person who isn't eligible for an SSN uses an ITIN when one is required for U.S. tax purposes. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/tin/itin/itin-supporting-documents?utm_source=openai))
- Escrow/title: California purchases normally involve escrow and title work. The escrow company handles the transaction and the title company can provide title insurance protecting against covered title defects. ([dre.ca.gov](https://www.dre.ca.gov/consumers/informationforhomebuyers.html?utm_source=openai))
- Ongoing taxes and insurance: You'll have Los Angeles-area property taxes and normally homeowners insurance, plus HOA dues if applicable.

One important distinction is that being allowed to own a Los Angeles home does not give you permission to live in the United States. Property ownership and U.S. immigration status are separate matters.

There are also tax issues worth planning for before deciding how to hold title. If you're a non-U.S. tax resident and rent the property, the rental income creates U.S. and potentially California tax considerations; California has specific withholding rules involving payments of California-source income to nonresidents. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay/withholding/withholding-on-nonresidents.html?utm_source=openai)) If you eventually sell as a foreign person, FIRPTA can require federal withholding from the sale proceeds. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai)) California also has its own real-estate-sale withholding regime. ([ftb.ca.gov](https://www.ftb.ca.gov/pay/withholding/real-estate-withholding.html?utm_source=openai))

If you're considering a fairly expensive Los Angeles property, it's particularly useful to decide before closing whether you should buy personally or through some other ownership structure. For foreign owners, that decision can affect U.S. estate tax, income tax, privacy, financing, and what happens when you eventually sell or transfer the property.

If you tell me your nationality/country of residence, approximate home price (e.g. $1M, $3M, $10M), whether you're paying cash or getting a mortgage, and whether it's a personal residence or investment property, I can lay out the likely documents, cash needed at closing, taxes, and ownership options.
